claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay asserts that Martin's style shows a high frequency of words of Anglo-Saxon origin.

claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay reports that the common Latin and Greek prefixes it lists are almost never found in Martin's work.

claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay argues that Martin reserves his rare neoclassical words for scenes whose speaker or setting is legalistic or learned, naming the maesters and the septons' court as the places they appear.

verdicts.trueWording: "a systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words"
verdicts.note: Abstract, para 1, verbatim: "distinguished not only by its pseudo-medieval setting... but by a systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words derived from Latin, Greek, French or other languages". Every limb (Latin, Greek, French) supported. Live page fetched raw, HTTP 200, browser UA.

verdicts.trueWording: "his style shows a high frequency of words of Anglo-Saxon origin"
verdicts.note: Abstract, para 2, verbatim: "Instead, his style shows a high frequency of words of Anglo-Saxon origin, a tendency which is particularly conspicuous in his use of compound and combination words." Live page raw fetch.

verdicts.trueWording: "Almost none of these are found in Martin's work."
verdicts.note: Section 'GRRM's PRACTICE / 1. George R.R. Martin's use of prefixes'. The page first reprints Dr Lam's Latin (ab-, ad-, inter-, intra-, post-, pre-, re-, sub-, super-) and Greek (a-, ana-, dia-, endo-, exo-, epi-, hyper-, hypo-) prefix lists, then says verbatim "Almost none of these are found in Martin's work. There are hardly if any words starting ab, sub, super, post... Their absence speaks volumes." Claim's 'almost never' limb matches; the essay itself grants exceptions (re-, submit, intermittent, fornication).

verdicts.trueWording: "deploying them carefully to distinguish scenes where he wants to accentuate"
verdicts.note: Section 3 (combining forms), verbatim: "...emphasises Martin's craft in deploying them carefully to distinguish scenes where he wants to accentuate the legalistic or learned character of the speaker or context of the setting." Both named venues are on the page: Maester Colemon's 'intercession' and the Oldtown maesters ('penetrate', 'complement', 'complaint'), and 'Fornication' in the chapter where Margaery is accused by the religious order of the septons (section 1 also cites 'chapters about the High Septon and his religious court').

verdicts.trueWording: "he conspicuously deploys the archaic prefix 'a-' to denote position: atop, abed, ahorse"
verdicts.note: Section 1, verbatim: "And sometimes Martin goes to the other extreme... delving beyond common speech into archaic native forms: for example, he conspicuously deploys the archaic prefix 'a-' to denote position: atop, abed, ahorse". All three exemplars and the native/archaic characterisation are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: "The result is to make his prose feel archaic."
verdicts.note: Section 'Some examples', verbatim, and the preceding sentence supplies the causal limb: "And they feel that much more ubiquitous because there are so few words sourced from Latin, Greek or French, few if any neoclassical affixes, no foreign combining forms. The result is to make his prose feel archaic." Note the sentence sits in 'Some examples', not the essay's CONCLUSION section, but the abstract makes the same conclusion.

verdicts.trueWording: "George R. R. Martin-8 Novels Dying of the Light Fevre Dream"
verdicts.note: books.google.com SearchWithinVolume2 (the URL the claim names) fetched raw, HTTP 200. p. 241 returns verbatim: "George R. R. Martin—8 Novels Dying of the Light Fevre Dream The Armageddon Rag A Game of Thrones... A Clash of Kings A Storm of Swords A Feast for Crows A Dance [with Dragons]" (the OCR interleaves the adjacent Cormac McCarthy column). 3 standalone novels + 5 ASOIAF volumes = the stated 8. p. 240 carries the running head of the same appendix. Evidence is Google Books' verbatim full-text index of pp. 240-241, not a page image.

verdicts.trueWording: "dragons, cloaks, unsullied" - p. 175 CINNAMON WORDS column
verdicts.note: p. 175 returns the string "dragons, cloaks, unsullied" verbatim, and the page header "CINNAMON WORDS NOD WORDS". Attribution to Martin is by column alignment on the same page: the author column (returned by q=George+R.+R.+Martin) runs Martin, McCarthy, McEwan, Mead, Melville, Meyer, Mitchell, Morrison, Nabokov, Orwell...; the cinnamon column runs "dragons, cloaks, unsullied / yessir, mam, upriver / lavatory, forwards, fridge / guardians, vampire, dorm / whale, forecastle, sperm / vampire, grimaced, flinched / mam, dint, piss / messed, navel, slop / mauve, banal, pun / beastly, quid, workhouse" - anchored decisively by Melville=whale/forecastle/sperm and Nabokov=mauve/banal/pun, so the first triple is Martin's. 'most anomalously often' matches the book's own gloss of cinnamon words (p. 170 "an approximation of their favorites", p. 172 "top three 'cinnamon words'", p. 166 discusses anomalous use).

verdicts.trueWording: p.172: fifty example authors PLUS "fifty more authors"; clichés not mentioned
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the quoted sentence covers the clichés table, and that the favourite-words table stops at the fifty - p. 172's very next sentence adds "fifty more authors of popular and critical acclaim", so that table covers a hundred
verdicts.note: The quotation is verbatim on p. 172: "...top three 'cinnamon words' and top three 'nod words' for each of the fifty authors I've been using as examples throughout this book. To add to the fun, I've also included fifty more authors of popular and critical acclaim." So the sentence is about the favourite-words (cinnamon/nod) table only - clichés are a different table on p. 158, worded differently ("fifty authors I use as examples, Number of Clichés per 100,000 Words"). The claim fuses two pages into one sentence and drops the second fifty. Route: books.google.com SearchWithinVolume2, the exact URL the claim names, fetched raw with a browser UA, HTTP 200 - Google Books' verbatim full-text index of the book, not a page image and not a third-party search snippet.

verdicts.trueWording: "Word Count (292,332)" - and the chapter rows sum to exactly 292,332
verdicts.note: Two independent raw routes, the live host having returned 403 to curl: (1) the wiki's own api.php action=parse prop=wikitext, HTTP 200, and (2) the Wayback raw capture web/20250521205534id_/, HTTP 200. Both carry the header row verbatim: "Character (9) | # of POVs (73) | % of Total POVs | Word Count (292,332) | % of Word Count". Locational nuance: the figure is printed in the Unique POV Breakdown header, not in the Chapter by Chapter table - but I summed the rendered chapter table myself and it is 73 rows totalling exactly 292,332, so the claim's limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: "Character (9)!!# of POVs (73)" - header of Unique POV Breakdown
verdicts.note: Verbatim in both routes: "# of POVs (73)" and "Character (9)" in the same header row. The table body lists exactly nine POV characters (Eddard, Catelyn, Daenerys, Tyrion, Jon, Bran, Sansa, Arya, Will) whose chapter counts 15+11+10+9+9+7+6+5+1 = 73, matching the chapter table's 73 rows (prologue + 72 chapters).

Verbatim in both routes. All three limbs on the page: 15 POV chapters, 53,467 words, 18.29% of word count. Cross-checked against the chapter table, which contains Eddard I through Eddard XV = 15 chapters.

"1,696" appears verbatim. I parsed all 73 rendered chapter rows: minimum 1,696 = Chapter 17 (Bran III), maximum 7,334 = Chapter 34 (Catelyn VI), exactly the two chapters the claim's page field names. Runners-up 7,214 (Eddard VII, ch. 30) and 7,100 (Tyrion VIII, ch. 62) confirm the maximum; the prologue's 3,801 is well above the minimum.
